clips.narration: This idea starts with a four-color quadrant brush at each point. Its trail changes with direction, overlap, rotation, and resolution. That makes the geometry visible. But a surviving pixel color is not, by itself, an arithmetic certificate of primality.

Z three means the third zeta zero, not twenty-three or a prime label. For the first hundred zero indices, negative starting slopes occurred at fourteen prime indices and thirty-five composite indices. Eleven prime indices sloped upward. Both signs mix the classes, so this proposed rule fails.

The proposed denominator, g of n, simplifies exactly to n. Substituting it into zeta's series leaves the same function where that series converges. The half inside g does not set s to one half. And ninety-seven and composite ninety-nine both have a fractional half when divided by two.

Zeta at one half exists and is about minus one point four six. The critical line instead uses one half plus i t. Particular heights give zeros. Putting ninety-seven into t gives a nonzero complex value. Fixing the real part does not identify an integer as prime.

With integer n used as height, ninety-seven and composite ninety-nine both occupy quadrant one. Comparing zeta at s, s plus one, and s minus one still fails. Matching ninety-seven's three colors keeps six primes and eighteen composites, while missing nineteen primes between two and one hundred.

Removing the unit term gives zeta minus one. Its zeros are where zeta equals one. Multiplying the two functions combines both zero sets. Every hypothetical off-line zeta zero survives, so the switch does not prove the hypothesis.

Reordering the same finite sum leaves its value unchanged. For the tested coefficient reversal, subtracting the reverse makes opposite positions have opposite signs. A nonzero, nonnegative composite indicator cannot have that symmetry. Other definitions of a backward recurrence would need a separate derivation.

Finite subtraction leaves nonprimes but requires knowing the prime terms to remove. At s equals minus one, the ordinary integer series diverges. Zeta's continued value, minus one twelfth, is not an ordinary sum for subtracting infinitely many primes.

For real s greater than one, define A as the odd-number part of zeta. Then A minus one minus log A cancels every odd-prime coefficient and leaves weighted odd composites. The coefficient at ninety-seven is zero; at ninety-nine it is one. Evaluating H at ninety-seven does not extract that coefficient.

Wilson's theorem tests a candidate without a list of previous primes. Our encoding places primes in quadrant one. The modular factorial supplies the answer; color displays it. This is not instantaneous. The separate four-divisor color test works only within its stated range.

Removing trivial factor pairs leaves an exact composite remainder. For odd integers greater than one, D counts nontrivial pairs: zero for ninety-seven, two for ninety-nine. The proof covers that entire domain. The implementation was independently checked through one hundred thousand. It still performs divisor counting.

The contribution is reproducible tests and counterexamples. Phase plots can guide searches; rigorous bounds must certify the zero count. Prime extraction also needs error bounds and cost comparisons. These experiments establish no new prime algorithm or Riemann Hypothesis advance.
